## Today's class

We'll estimate π with a small Monte Carlo simulation and run the same code in three places: on your laptop, on one CHPC node, and across several nodes with a Slurm job array. You'll write the first two versions yourself. For the job array, you can leverage Codex to write the scripts and you check them before submitting. Since we know the answer, it's easy to tell whether each version is correct, and we'll also measure how much faster it gets as we add cores.

Please work in pairs. Your answers, prompts, and timings go into `lab11.qmd`; the step-by-step instructions are in [Lab 11](lab.qmd).

# Estimating π

## The idea

Throw $N$ random points into the square $[-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]$ and count how many land inside the unit circle. The square has area 4 and the circle has area $\pi$, so that proportion estimates $\pi / 4$:

$$
\hat p = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \mathbf{1}\left(x_j^2 + y_j^2 \le 1\right),
\qquad
\hat \pi = 4 \hat p .
$$

```{r}
#| label: dots
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: 50%
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-cap: "2,000 random points. Blue points fall inside the unit circle."
set.seed(2312)
dots <- data.frame(x = runif(2000, -1, 1), y = runif(2000, -1, 1))
dots$inside <- with(dots, x^2 + y^2 <= 1)
ggplot(dots, aes(x, y, colour = inside)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .6, size = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "steelblue", `FALSE` = "tomato"),
                      guide = "none") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = sprintf("pi-hat = 4 x %.3f = %.3f",
                       mean(dots$inside), 4 * mean(dots$inside))) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## How precise is the estimate?

Each point lands inside the circle with probability $p = \pi/4$, so the standard error of $\hat\pi$ is

$$
\text{SE}(\hat \pi) = 4\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{N}} \approx \frac{1.64}{\sqrt N}.
$$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Where does this formula come from?

Each point is a yes/no trial: it lands in the circle or it doesn't. Let $Z_j = \mathbf{1}(x_j^2 + y_j^2 \le 1)$. The probability that $Z_j = 1$ is the area of the circle divided by the area of the square,

$$
p = \frac{\pi \cdot 1^2}{2 \times 2} = \frac{\pi}{4} \approx 0.785,
$$

so $Z_j$ is Bernoulli with mean $p$ and variance $p(1-p)$.

The proportion inside the circle, $\hat p$, is the average of $N$ independent $Z_j$'s, so its variance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat p) = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{j=1}^N \operatorname{Var}(Z_j) = \frac{p(1-p)}{N}.
$$

Since $\hat\pi = 4\hat p$, the variance gets multiplied by $4^2 = 16$:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\pi) = \frac{16\, p(1-p)}{N}, \qquad \text{SE}(\hat\pi) = 4\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{N}}.
$$

With $p = \pi/4$ we get $p(1-p) \approx 0.1686$ and $4\sqrt{0.1686} \approx 1.64$, which gives $1.64/\sqrt N$.

In our simulation, every replicate has the same number of points $n$. The mean of the `nsims` replicate estimates is therefore the same as the estimate from all $N = \texttt{nsims} \times n$ points together, and the formula holds with that $N$. You can check this on your own run: `sd(ans) / sqrt(nsims)` should come out close to $1.64 / \sqrt N$.

In the plot below I used the true value of π to draw the band. In a real problem you don't know $p$, so you would plug in $\hat p$ instead, or use the spread of the replicates.
:::

```{r}
#| label: convergence
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Point estimate of π (running estimate from one million points), with a ±2 SE band around the true value. "
set.seed(123)
N <- 1e6
inside <- (runif(N, -1, 1)^2 + runif(N, -1, 1)^2) <= 1
keep <- unique(round(10^seq(2, 6, length.out = 400)))
conv <- data.frame(N = keep, pihat = 4 * cumsum(inside)[keep] / keep)
conv$se <- 4 * sqrt((pi / 4) * (1 - pi / 4) / conv$N)
ggplot(conv, aes(N, pihat)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = pi - 2 * se, ymax = pi + 2 * se),
              fill = "steelblue", alpha = .2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = pi, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Number of points (log scale)", y = expression(hat(pi))) +
  theme_minimal()
```

With a million points the SE is about 0.0016, so we can trust roughly 3.14. To get one more correct digit we need the SE to shrink by a factor of 10, and because of the square root that means 100 times as many points. A few more digits and your laptop is no longer enough.

## Setting up the simulation

We run `nsims` replicates with `n` points each and average them. Each replicate gets its own seed. Replicate 17 then always draws the same numbers, whether it runs first or last, on your laptop or on a node at CHPC.

```{r}
#| label: simpi-code
#| file: scripts/simpi.R
#| eval: true
```

`make_seeds()` gives each replicate its own starting point in R's random-number generator. The starting points are far apart, so no two replicates ever use the same random numbers. Before drawing any points, `simpi()` jumps to replicate `i`'s own starting point. That's why the final π̂ doesn't depend on how the work is split up.

## The known answer

The result is that every correct version of the simulation prints the same number (down to the last digit). Here it is with the default size, 10,000 replicates of 10,000 points:

```{r}
#| label: known-answer
#| echo: true
seeds <- make_seeds(10000)

serial   <- sapply(1:10000, simpi, n = 10000, seeds = seeds)
parallel <- unlist(parallel::mclapply(1:10000, simpi, n = 10000,
                                      seeds = seeds, mc.cores = 2))

sprintf("%.12f", c(serial = mean(serial), parallel = mean(parallel)))
```

We'll use this number all day as a check, including on the code Codex writes. If a version of the simulation prints something different, it has a bug.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}

## Looking back at Hands-on 1

If $T_k$ is the wall time on $k$ cores, the speedup is $S_k = T_1 / T_k$ and the efficiency is $E_k = S_k / k$. On 4 cores you probably got a speedup a bit below 4 (I got about 3.7 on my laptop). Starting the workers and collecting their results takes time, the cores don't all finish at the same moment, and your laptop is doing other things too. For the whole job, there's also work that runs on a single core however many you have: starting R and saving the results. The times the scripts print leave those out, but `sacct` on CHPC includes them, so you'll see them in the scaling report. Amdahl's law [@amdahlValiditySingleProcessor1967] puts a number on this: if a fraction $f$ of the work can run in parallel, then $S_k \le 1 / \left((1-f) + f/k\right)$.

The other thing to notice is how `02-mclapply.R` decides how many cores to use. When you write `--cpus-per-task=4`, Slurm sets aside 4 cores for you, but R has no idea. So the script asks:

``` r
ncores <- as.integer(Sys.getenv("SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"))
```

You might be tempted to use `parallel::detectCores()` instead. On a cluster that counts all the cores on the node, including the ones other people are using, so you could end up starting 64 processes on the 4 cores you were given.

# Many nodes with job arrays

## Job arrays

A job array runs the same script several times. Each run is called a task. Tasks can land on different nodes, and each task can find out which one it is from a few environment variables.

``` bash
#SBATCH --array=1-4          # 4 tasks
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4    # each task gets 4 cores
#SBATCH --output=%x-%A_%a.out
```

| Variable                     | Meaning                | Example       |
|------------------------------|------------------------|---------------|
| `SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID` (`%A`)  | ID shared by all tasks | 1234567       |
| `SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID` (`%a`) | This task's number     | 1, 2, 3, or 4 |
| `SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT`     | Number of tasks        | 4             |
| `SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK`        | Cores for this task    | 4             |

Four tasks with 4 cores each is 16 cores, and none of them has to wait for a node with 16 free cores.

## Splitting the work

One simple way to split the replicates is to give task `a` (out of `T`) the replicates `a, a + T, a + 2T`, and so on:

```{r}
#| label: split
#| echo: true
nsims <- 10; ntasks <- 4
lapply(1:ntasks, function(a) seq(a, nsims, by = ntasks))
```

Each task runs its share with `mclapply()` on its own cores, using the same seeds as before, and saves the results in its own file (`results/pi-task001.rds`, `results/pi-task002.rds`, ...). If all tasks wrote to the same file, they would overwrite each other.

## Putting the results together

A second job reads all the files, puts the replicates back in order, and takes the mean. You don't have to wait and submit it by hand; Slurm can hold it until the whole array has finished:

``` bash
jid=$(sbatch --parsable 03-array.slurm)            # --parsable prints only the job ID
sbatch --dependency=afterok:$jid 04-aggregate.slurm # starts once every task succeeded
```

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart LR
  S["sbatch 03-array.slurm"] --> T1["task 1<br>4 cores"]
  S --> T2["task 2<br>4 cores"]
  S --> T3["task 3<br>4 cores"]
  S --> T4["task 4<br>4 cores"]
  T1 --> R["results/pi-task00*.rds"]
  T2 --> R
  T3 --> R
  T4 --> R
  R --> A["04-aggregate.slurm<br>(afterok)"]
  A --> P["pi-hat"]
```

Slurm decides where the tasks run. On a shared partition, several of them may end up on the same node, so have each task record its host name (`Sys.info()[["nodename"]]`) and you'll know.

## Coding agents on CHPC

A quick reminder from Tuesday. `module load codex` makes Codex available in your terminal session, and `codex` starts it in the current folder. It starts with a system prompt written by CHPC, so it already knows about the cluster, the modules, and Slurm. CHPC has also given it some skills. The two that matter today are `job-triage`, for figuring out why a job failed, and `slurm-utilization-audit`, for checking whether a job used what it asked for. Codex runs with your permissions, but CHPC blocks some commands, such as `rm`, and it has no network access.

On top of that, the `AGENTS.md` file in your lab folder adds a few rules for this lab. The most important one is that Codex doesn't submit jobs; it writes them and you submit them. Before you ask it for anything, write down how you'll check the result. You can always compare against the known answer. And, as in Lab 08, keep a log of your prompts.

If you run out of Codex tokens, `module load codex_CHPC_local_model` gives you the same interface with a model that runs at CHPC.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}

# Reference (read at home)

## Submitting without a `.slurm` file

For a quick one-off job, `sbatch --wrap` builds the batch script for you:

``` bash
sbatch --account=notchpeak-shared-short --partition=notchpeak-shared-short \
  --time=00:10:00 --mem=2G --job-name=01-sapply \
  --wrap="module load R; Rscript --vanilla 01-sapply.R"
```

I still recommend a `.slurm` file for anything you'll run again. It's a record of what you asked for.

## Interactive sessions

If you need to debug on a compute node instead of the login node, start an interactive session with `salloc`:

``` bash
salloc --account=notchpeak-shared-short --partition=notchpeak-shared-short \
  --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=4G --time=00:30:00
module load R
R
```

Type `exit` when you're done so the cores go back to the pool. Interactive sessions are good for poking around, not for long runs.

## Slurm options worth knowing

Keep in mind that Slurm only reserves resources. Whether your program actually uses them is your job.

| Option | What it does |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `--ntasks` | Number of processes (tasks); they may be on different nodes. Default is 1. |
| `--cpus-per-task` | Cores per task, always on the same node. This is the one for `mclapply()` and OpenMP. |
| `--nodes` | Number of nodes. You rarely need it for R. |
| `--mem` / `--mem-per-cpu` | Memory per node or per core. A job that uses more is killed (`OUT_OF_MEMORY`). |
| `--time` | Time limit. A job that runs longer is killed (`TIMEOUT`). |
| `--account` + `--partition` | Who pays, and which machines. They have to go together. |
| `--array` | Runs the script as several tasks of one job. |
| `--output` | Log file. `%x` is the job name, `%j` the job ID, `%A`/`%a` the array job and task IDs. |

`mychpc batch` lists the account/partition combinations you can use. For this class, `notchpeak-shared-short` (it is both the account and the partition name) is meant for short jobs and usually starts quickly, so we use it today. The class account `phs7045` with `notchpeak-shared-freecycle` gives you more resources, but your job can be stopped when the owners of the nodes need them.

## Good habits

- Set `--time`, `--mem`, and `--cpus-per-task` yourself and ask for roughly what you need. Afterwards, `sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,TotalCPU,MaxRSS,State` tells you what the job actually used.
- Try a tiny version first, then scale up.
- Large temporary files go in scratch (`/scratch/general/vast/$USER`), not your home directory.
- Don't run computations on the login nodes. Compiling and quick tests are fine.
- Don't use `detectCores()` on the cluster, and don't let several tasks write to the same file.
- Thousands of jobs that each run for a few seconds are slow overall, because waiting in the queue and starting R take longer than the work. Give each task a decent amount of work.

## Aliases

These save some typing. Put them in `~/.bash_profile` on CHPC:

``` bash
alias sq="squeue --me"
sa() {
  sacct -j "$1" --format=JobID,JobName,Partition,State,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,TotalCPU,MaxRSS,NodeList -X
}
```
